theory.text: Beginners tend to skip straight to the prompt. Open the editor, type, wait. Sometimes it works. More often it doesn't — and the reason isn't the model, it's the process. Vibe coders who get reliable results carry a small mental checklist: three questions to answer before writing, two things to do after receiving the response. It's not bureaucracy — it's how you avoid wasting ten sessions on something that could have gone right on the first try.

Before every new session, pause on three questions: What exactly does this feature need to do? — not vaguely, but with a precise input and output. Are there constraints the AI can't know on its own? — stack, libraries already in use, patterns already adopted. What should it not touch? — the parts that already work and must not be rewritten. If you can answer all three before opening the prompt, what you write will already be far more targeted.
💡 Before generating code, ask for a plan. "Describe how you'd structure this feature — files involved, main logic. Don't write code yet." A 10-line text plan saves hours of debugging.

theory.prompt: Before implementing: describe how you'd structure an email notification system for new orders. Files involved, main logic. Wait before writing code.
theory.output:
Proposed structure:
- /lib/emails/order-notification.ts → template and sending logic
- /api/webhooks/new-order.ts → trigger after order creation
- Would use Resend, already configured in the project

Key detail: the notification should only fire if payment is confirmed, not at the moment the order is created. Shall I confirm before proceeding?

theory.text: When the AI returns code, the checklist isn't done — it's halfway. Before moving on: test immediately, don't put it off. Skim the diff, even just diagonally — you're looking for something unexpected, a file that wasn't supposed to be touched, a dependency quietly added. If everything holds up, commit. One commit per working step is the safety net that lets you take bigger risks on the next one.

The checklist is a tool, not a ritual. For small corrections — "move this button to the right", "change the color of this text" — skipping it is the right call. It's worth pausing only when a session has real scope: a new feature, a refactor, an integration. Not every single prompt.
🔑 Before every session that matters: what it needs to do, what it must not touch, show me the plan first. After: test, skim the diff, commit. That's all.

exercise.prompt_template: Before asking the AI to write code, always ask for a [BLANK] first — it saves you hours of [BLANK].

blanks.hint_1: What do you ask for before someone starts building something complex?
blanks.hint_2: One word, starts with 'p' — it's what you do before you act.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'plan'. Asking for a plan before code is the single most effective move in the loop: it stops misunderstandings before they become bugs.

blanks.hint_1: What's waiting for you if you skip the plan and the code goes wrong?
blanks.hint_2: The activity you do when something doesn't work and you're hunting for the reason.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'debugging' (or 'rewrites', 'corrections'). A preventive plan dramatically reduces the time spent chasing errors in generated code.

outro.recap: The vibe coder's checklist is simple: three questions before every session, a plan before the code, test and commit after every step that works.
outro.next_prompt: Path 1 complete. Next stop: Path 2 — we start building truly effective prompts, beginning with what makes them work from the inside.
